screens.title: CPU Performance Monitoring and Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on understanding how a Linux system spends C P U time and how to diagnose real performance issues. You will learn to use live tools like top and htop to see which processes are active now, and use mpstat and sar to inspect per-core behavior and historical trends. Knowing the difference between user C P U time, kernel time, and input and output wait is essential: high C P U doesn't always mean the C P U is the problem. For example, high input and output wait points you to disks, while a single core pegged at 100 percent suggests a single-threaded workload. This chapter teaches practical commands and a repeatable workflow: observe, identify the offending processes or cores, then choose the right next step, whether that is profiling the app, checking storage input and output, or investigating virtualization steal time. By the end, you will be able to decide if the C P U needs optimization or if another subsystem is the true bottleneck.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Learning Objectives
Troubleshooting workflow
A quick, practical sequence for CPU issues.
1. Observe
Use top/htop to see CPU states and active PIDs. Note load averages and which state is high.
2. Inspect cores
Run mpstat -P ALL to detect per-core saturation or imbalance.
3. Trend
Query sar for historical context to confirm whether the issue is persistent.
4. Act
Profile the process, check I/O, or address hypervisor contention depending on the evidence.
Common indicators and their likely cause
High iowait
Usually indicates disk I/O bottlenecks; check disk metrics and iostat.
High system time
Suggests kernel work or drivers; consider strace or perf for deeper inspection.
High steal time
Indicates hypervisor resource contention; coordinate with the host operator.

screens.title: Understanding top and its CPU state line
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define what the C P U(s) line reports and why each field matters. The C P U(s) breakdown shows how the system's time is split across categories: user time is spent running regular application code; system time is consumed by the kernel for device drivers and system calls; nice is user code with lower scheduling priority; idle is when the C P U has no work; iowait is idle time spent while waiting for input and output operations to complete; hardware and software interrupts represent time servicing interrupts; steal time appears when a hypervisor takes cycles away from a virtual machine. For example, if you see high user time on a database during peak queries, that is expected and indicates the C P U is doing productive work. But if iowait is high while C P U idle is also high, that points to storage slowness: the C P U is waiting for data, not computing. A common misconception is treating any high total C P U as a C P U bottleneck; instead, break down the time to understand whether you need to profile code, tune kernel settings, investigate storage, or speak to the virtual host team. As a takeaway, always ask: what category is high and what subsystem does that implicate?

keyIdea.text: Break down CPU time into categories to map symptoms to subsystems—application, kernel, I/O, or hypervisor.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Understanding top
Cpu(s) breakdown
Read these percentages to determine where time is spent.
us — user time
Time running application code. High during compute-heavy workloads.
sy — system time
Time in kernel mode for drivers and system calls. Excessive values suggest kernel or driver issues.
wa — iowait
CPU idle but waiting for I/O completion. High wa usually means a disk I/O bottleneck, not CPU compute pressure.
st — steal
Cycles stolen by a hypervisor. If high, your VM is being starved of CPU by the host configuration or oversubscription.
Example top snippet
%Cpu(s): 12.3 us,  3.6 sy,  0.0 ni, 82.7 id,  1.4 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
Interpretation
Most time is idle; small user time indicates light application work. If wa were high, focus on storage.
Key takeaway
Always map each high percentage to the subsystem it implicates; that guides the next diagnostic tool.

screens.title: top vs htop
screens.narratorSegment: Both top and htop show live process and C P U information, but they serve different workflows. top is ubiquitous and available on minimal systems; it reports a concise table with C P U states and processes. htop is an enhanced interactive viewer that colors C P U bars per core, supports easier sorting, and allows process actions like renice or kill with simple keys. Use top when you need a minimal, always-available interface in a recovery shell or script-friendly environment. Use htop when you want rapid visual scanning of all cores or to filter and act on processes quickly. For example, when a single PID spikes to ninety percent, top will show the PID and percentage; htop will also draw that core's bar and let you highlight the process more easily. A common misconception is thinking htop provides more data than top—both expose the same kernel metrics; htop just improves discoverability. Choosing between them is about access and speed: pick top for portability and htop for interactive diagnostics. top vs htop means top for ubiquity and scripting; htop for rapid interactive triage and per-core visualization.. In practical terms, when to use each tool and what they reveal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Identifying the CPU-hungry process
screens.narratorSegment: When troubleshooting you must quickly identify the process or kernel task responsible for high C P U. Start with top or htop and sort by C P U usage to reveal the top consumers. Note the PID, command name, and the C P U percentage. For a concrete example, imagine a web worker pegging at ninety percent user time. In top you'll see the PID and C P U percent; in htop you'll also see which logical core is saturated. Once you have the PID, inspect the process user, recent logs, and whether the process is expected to be busy. If it's an application process, consider profiling or checking for runaway loops in its code or configuration. If the high consumer is a kernel thread, the approach changes: use tools like strace to watch system calls for a user-space process or perf for system-wide profiling. A common trap is killing the obvious process without understanding whether it is a symptom; always check whether the process is legitimately working on expected load, such as a backup or heavy query. The takeaway is to collect evidence—PID, owner, C P U state, and recent logs—before deciding to stop or profile.

Live command examples
# Start top and sort by CPU
top

Quick verification steps
  • Record the PID, CPU%, and owner.
  • Check process logs and configuration for expected high load.
  • If suspect, use strace for system-call-heavy processes or perf for CPU hotspots.
Scenario card
Example: a worker process PID 4213 shows 95% user time during a nightly batch. Logs show repeated retries. This suggests an application loop; profiling or code fixes are appropriate before a blind restart.
Common mistake
Killing the top CPU process immediately can disrupt legitimate work. Confirm role and impact first.
Key takeaway
Identify PID and context, then choose profiling, configuration change, or controlled restart.

screens.title: mpstat — per-core visibility
screens.narratorSegment: mpstat reports processor statistics per logical C P U which helps you spot imbalances. Use mpstat with the -P ALL option to report every C P U's user, system, idle and wait times. For example, run mpstat with one-second intervals to observe a workload: if core zero reads one hundred percent user while others are mostly idle, the application is single-threaded and cannot benefit from additional cores. That tells you whether to optimize the application or scale horizontally. Another concrete example: a parallel worker should show fairly even user time across cores; if it doesn't, investigate scheduling or affinity settings. A common misunderstanding is assuming a high overall C P U means all cores are full; mpstat proves whether the load is concentrated. When reading mpstat, look for consistent per-core saturation rather than brief spikes. If one core is constantly pegged, profiling that specific thread or checking for C P U affinity constraints is the correct follow-up. The key insight: per-core data pinpoints whether you face parallelism limits or system-wide C P U pressure. mpstat — per-core visibility means mpstat -p all reveals whether load is balanced or concentrated on a single core, guiding whether to profile code or scale differently.. In practical terms, detecting single-core saturation and multi-core distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › mpstat per-core
Command example
mpstat -P ALL 1 5  # show per-CPU stats every 1s for 5 samples
What to look for
  • One core at 100% user time: single-threaded saturation.
  • All cores high: system-wide CPU pressure or highly parallel workload.
  • High system on a few cores: kernel activity concentrated by IRQ affinity or drivers.
Scenario and action
If mpstat shows one core saturated, examine application threading, check affinity settings, or consider running multiple instances to utilize other cores.
Misconception
Assuming more cores always improve performance. Some workloads are inherently single-threaded and require redesign to gain parallel benefit.
Key takeaway
Per-core stats reveal whether to optimize code, adjust affinity, or scale horizontally.

screens.title: sar — historical CPU trends
screens.narratorSegment: sar collects and reports historical C P U utilization, which is invaluable when you need to know if high C P U was a temporary spike or a recurring problem. Running sar -u with sampling intervals shows C P U user, system, idle, and iowait over time. For example, schedule sysstat collection and later use sar -u -f against a specific day to inspect periods of sustained high user time that correspond with scheduled jobs. This helps you differentiate between a nightly batch that intentionally uses C P U and an unexpected sustained load. Another example: if sar shows repeated hourly spikes of high iowait, the pattern suggests an input and output-bound cron job or backup that should be rescheduled or optimized. A common mistake is relying solely on live tools that capture only the current state; sar gives you the timeline context needed to make better decisions. The practical implication is that trend data tells you whether to tune the scheduler, adjust maintenance windows, or provision additional resources. sar — historical CPU trends means use sar to determine if cpu patterns are scheduled or recurring, guiding timing and provisioning decisions.. Command examples

sar -u 5 3

# View saved data for day XX
sar -u -f /var/log/sysstat/saXX
Use cases
  • Confirm whether high CPU is sustained across hours or days
  • Correlate CPU trends with cron jobs, backups, or traffic patterns
Scenario
If sar shows a nightly sustained rise in user time corresponding to backups, you might reschedule the job or throttle concurrency instead of changing application code.
Misconception
Assuming a single observation equals a trend. Always check historical data before major changes.
Key takeaway
Use sar to separate transient spikes from recurring load and to plan corrective actions with confidence.

screens.title: Common CPU-related bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of common C P U-related bottlenecks you will repeatedly encounter. First, a single-threaded application on a multi-core host can saturate one core while others remain idle; mpstat helps detect this. Second, excessive context switching occurs when many short-lived tasks compete, causing the kernel to spend time switching state rather than doing productive work; high context switch rates from tools like vmstat signal this. Third, kernel overhead or driver issues manifest as high system time, which may require strace or perf to diagnose. Fourth, virtualization steal time shows when a hypervisor preempts your VM to run other guests; a high steal percentage means you must consult the host operator or adjust VM sizing. For a concrete example, a web server with a threaded worker model should show load distributed across cores; if it does not, the application might be single-threaded, or C P U affinity may be misconfigured. A common mistake is treating high total C P U as a reason to add cores when the real fix is reducing context switching or addressing input and output bottlenecks. The practical approach is to use the right evidence to select profiling, tuning, or scaling.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Common CPU bottlenecks
Bottleneck list
Single-threaded saturation
One core at 100% while others idle; consider profiling or scaling horizontally.
Excessive context switching
High cs rate wastes CPU on switching; reduce thread count or batch tasks.
Kernel overhead
High sy time may point to drivers, system calls, or kernel-side inefficiencies; use perf.
Virtualization steal
High st percentage means host is oversubscribed; coordinate with the host operator.
Concrete scenario
An analytics job runs nightly and saturates one core; mpstat shows one core at 100 percent. The correct action is to profile the job or split the workload, not to immediately add cores to the host.
Key takeaway
Map symptoms to this taxonomy so your remediation targets the real cause, not a surface metric.

screens.title: Troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A structured workflow reduces guesswork. Start with live observation: run top or htop and note C P U states, load averages, and the top PIDs. Next, inspect per-core metrics with mpstat to see whether load is balanced or concentrated. If you need history, query sar to understand timing and recurrence. Based on these findings, decide your next action. If a single process is thrashing the C P U, collect logs and profile the application. If iowait is high, investigate disks with iostat and sar -b. If system time is high, use strace on suspect processes or perf for system-wide hotspots. If steal time is high, coordinate with the virtualization host. For an example sequence: observe top showing high iowait, run iostat to confirm disk saturation, then check which processes are issuing heavy input and output. A common pitfall is skipping the evidence step and immediately tuning or restarting services; that can mask the root cause. The essential idea is to gather the minimal set of facts that points unambiguously to the subsystem you must fix. Troubleshooting workflow means observe, inspect per-core, check history, then act with profiling or subsystem-specific tools.. In practical terms, a repeatable, evidence-driven path from observation to action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Lab walkthrough: simulating and diagnosing CPU load
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence shows how to simulate a C P U load and diagnose it. First, prepare two terminals. In the first, run top or htop to observe the C P U(s) line and load averages. In the second, start a C P U-intensive workload such as the stress tool configured to use multiple workers for a short period. For example, start four C P U workers for sixty seconds. Immediately return to the monitoring terminal and observe the jump in user time and the drop in idle time. Then run mpstat -P ALL to see whether all logical CPUs are active. If all cores rise evenly, your workload parallelizes well. If only one core spikes, it is single-threaded. After the stress completes or you stop it, confirm C P U usage returns to baseline. A common pitfall is not having permission or missing the stress package; when that's the case, a simple infinite loop in the background can simulate C P U work, but it may only affect a single core. The learning goal is to connect the simulated action to observable metric changes so you can reproduce and diagnose real production behavior with confidence.

screens.title: When to escalate: kernel profiling and virtualization
screens.narratorSegment: Some situations require deeper inspection or escalation. When system time is high, that points to kernel-level activity. Use strace on a suspect user-space process to see if it is making many expensive system calls; this helps when sy is elevated. For system-wide or hard-to-isolate kernel work, use perf to sample where C P U cycles go across the system and identify hotspots in kernel code or drivers. In virtualized environments, a high steal percentage is evidence the hypervisor is oversubscribed and you are being starved of cycles; resolving that requires cooperation with the host operator or changing instance size. A concrete example: if perf samples show a kernel driver function consuming cycles during high sy, you may update the driver or change hardware configuration. A common misconception is to assume the problem is always inside the VM; stealing can make a VM appear C P U-starved even when its guest processes are idle. The practical rule: local profiling first, then escalate with evidence to the host admin or vendor when the problem is outside your VM's control. screens.title: Interpreting sample top output
screens.narratorSegment: Let's practice interpreting a sample C P U(s) line and deciding an initial action. Suppose top reports: five percent user, two percent system, eighty percent idle, and thirteen percent iowait. The dominant iowait indicates the C P U is idle but waiting for disk operations. The correct initial action is to investigate disk input and output rather than attempting to add C P U. Tools like iostat or sar -b will show which devices and processes are issuing heavy input and output. Contrast that with a report where user time is very high across all cores; that suggests the C P U is genuinely under compute load and profiling or scaling compute is appropriate. Another example: a core at one hundred percent user with low overall load average often means a single-threaded process; consider optimizing that process or running multiple instances. A common learner mistake is to conflate high total percentage with C P U compute requirement. The practical rule is to map the highest categories to subsystem checks: iowait→storage, sy→kernel, st→hypervisor. Interpreting sample top output means map high percentages to subsystems and choose targeted next steps instead of assumptions.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on understanding how a Linux system spends C P U time and how to diagnose real performance issues. You will learn to use live tools like top and htop to see which processes are active now, and use mpstat and sar to inspect per-core behavior and historical trends. Knowing the difference between user C P U time, kernel time, and input and output wait is essential: high C P U doesn't always mean the C P U is the problem. For example, high input and output wait points you to disks, while a single core pegged at 100 percent suggests a single-threaded workload. This chapter teaches practical commands and a repeatable workflow: observe, identify the offending processes or cores, then choose the right next step, whether that is profiling the app, checking storage input and output, or investigating virtualization steal time. By the end, you will be able to decide if the C P U needs optimization or if another subsystem is the true bottleneck.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to run live inspection tools, interpret C P U states, and choose the right next diagnostic steps. First, you'll use top and htop to read live C P U usage and identify which processes are consuming cycles. For example, you'll locate a process with sustained high C P U and decide whether to profile or restart it. Second, you'll read C P U state metrics such as user time, system time, and input and output wait, and learn how a high input and output wait points to storage issues instead of a C P U bottleneck. Third, you'll use mpstat to check per-core utilization to detect single-threaded saturation. Finally, you'll query historical reports with sar to understand whether high C P U is a transient spike or a sustained trend. Each objective pairs a command with a decision: observe, interpret, act. These are practical skills you will repeatedly apply when a system feels slow, and they reduce time-to-resolution by focusing effort where it matters.

This second objectives screen focuses on diagnosing the root cause and acting appropriately. You will learn to differentiate symptoms that suggest application-level C P U pressure from symptoms that point to kernel or input and output issues. For example, a high system time suggests kernel activity such as device drivers or excessive system calls; in that case you would investigate kernel threads or use a system profiler. You will also learn to detect virtualized-host contention via steal time and know when to escalate to the hypervisor owner. Another objective is to identify excessive context switching, which appears as a high context switch rate and often indicates too many threads or short-lived processes. Practically, you will practice the initial troubleshooting workflow: identify heavy processes, check logs and configuration, profile code if needed, and consider scaling or tuning. Each objective emphasizes making the right next diagnostic decision quickly.

Let's define what the C P U(s) line reports and why each field matters. The C P U(s) breakdown shows how the system's time is split across categories: user time is spent running regular application code; system time is consumed by the kernel for device drivers and system calls; nice is user code with lower scheduling priority; idle is when the C P U has no work; iowait is idle time spent while waiting for input and output operations to complete; hardware and software interrupts represent time servicing interrupts; steal time appears when a hypervisor takes cycles away from a virtual machine. For example, if you see high user time on a database during peak queries, that is expected and indicates the C P U is doing productive work. But if iowait is high while C P U idle is also high, that points to storage slowness: the C P U is waiting for data, not computing. A common misconception is treating any high total C P U as a C P U bottleneck; instead, break down the time to understand whether you need to profile code, tune kernel settings, investigate storage, or speak to the virtual host team. As a takeaway, always ask: what category is high and what subsystem does that implicate?

Both top and htop show live process and C P U information, but they serve different workflows. top is ubiquitous and available on minimal systems; it reports a concise table with C P U states and processes. htop is an enhanced interactive viewer that colors C P U bars per core, supports easier sorting, and allows process actions like renice or kill with simple keys. Use top when you need a minimal, always-available interface in a recovery shell or script-friendly environment. Use htop when you want rapid visual scanning of all cores or to filter and act on processes quickly. For example, when a single PID spikes to ninety percent, top will show the PID and percentage; htop will also draw that core's bar and let you highlight the process more easily. A common misconception is thinking htop provides more data than top—both expose the same kernel metrics; htop just improves discoverability. Choosing between them is about access and speed: pick top for portability and htop for interactive diagnostics. top vs htop means top for ubiquity and scripting; htop for rapid interactive triage and per-core visualization.. In practical terms, when to use each tool and what they reveal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When troubleshooting you must quickly identify the process or kernel task responsible for high C P U. Start with top or htop and sort by C P U usage to reveal the top consumers. Note the PID, command name, and the C P U percentage. For a concrete example, imagine a web worker pegging at ninety percent user time. In top you'll see the PID and C P U percent; in htop you'll also see which logical core is saturated. Once you have the PID, inspect the process user, recent logs, and whether the process is expected to be busy. If it's an application process, consider profiling or checking for runaway loops in its code or configuration. If the high consumer is a kernel thread, the approach changes: use tools like strace to watch system calls for a user-space process or perf for system-wide profiling. A common trap is killing the obvious process without understanding whether it is a symptom; always check whether the process is legitimately working on expected load, such as a backup or heavy query. The takeaway is to collect evidence—PID, owner, C P U state, and recent logs—before deciding to stop or profile.

mpstat reports processor statistics per logical C P U which helps you spot imbalances. Use mpstat with the -P ALL option to report every C P U's user, system, idle and wait times. For example, run mpstat with one-second intervals to observe a workload: if core zero reads one hundred percent user while others are mostly idle, the application is single-threaded and cannot benefit from additional cores. That tells you whether to optimize the application or scale horizontally. Another concrete example: a parallel worker should show fairly even user time across cores; if it doesn't, investigate scheduling or affinity settings. A common misunderstanding is assuming a high overall C P U means all cores are full; mpstat proves whether the load is concentrated. When reading mpstat, look for consistent per-core saturation rather than brief spikes. If one core is constantly pegged, profiling that specific thread or checking for C P U affinity constraints is the correct follow-up. The key insight: per-core data pinpoints whether you face parallelism limits or system-wide C P U pressure. mpstat — per-core visibility means mpstat -p all reveals whether load is balanced or concentrated on a single core, guiding whether to profile code or scale differently.. In practical terms, detecting single-core saturation and multi-core distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

sar collects and reports historical C P U utilization, which is invaluable when you need to know if high C P U was a temporary spike or a recurring problem. Running sar -u with sampling intervals shows C P U user, system, idle, and iowait over time. For example, schedule sysstat collection and later use sar -u -f against a specific day to inspect periods of sustained high user time that correspond with scheduled jobs. This helps you differentiate between a nightly batch that intentionally uses C P U and an unexpected sustained load. Another example: if sar shows repeated hourly spikes of high iowait, the pattern suggests an input and output-bound cron job or backup that should be rescheduled or optimized. A common mistake is relying solely on live tools that capture only the current state; sar gives you the timeline context needed to make better decisions. The practical implication is that trend data tells you whether to tune the scheduler, adjust maintenance windows, or provision additional resources. sar — historical CPU trends means use sar to determine if cpu patterns are scheduled or recurring, guiding timing and provisioning decisions.. In practical terms, using sar to confirm whether high cpu is transient or persistent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are a handful of common C P U-related bottlenecks you will repeatedly encounter. First, a single-threaded application on a multi-core host can saturate one core while others remain idle; mpstat helps detect this. Second, excessive context switching occurs when many short-lived tasks compete, causing the kernel to spend time switching state rather than doing productive work; high context switch rates from tools like vmstat signal this. Third, kernel overhead or driver issues manifest as high system time, which may require strace or perf to diagnose. Fourth, virtualization steal time shows when a hypervisor preempts your VM to run other guests; a high steal percentage means you must consult the host operator or adjust VM sizing. For a concrete example, a web server with a threaded worker model should show load distributed across cores; if it does not, the application might be single-threaded, or C P U affinity may be misconfigured. A common mistake is treating high total C P U as a reason to add cores when the real fix is reducing context switching or addressing input and output bottlenecks. The practical approach is to use the right evidence to select profiling, tuning, or scaling.
